extracted.intended_audience: children's book authors, illustrators, agents, editors, publishers, and readers interested in inclusive representation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and industry critique about authentic, inclusive disability representation in children's and middle grade publishing, addressing creators, gatekeepers, conferences, and production/accessibility practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish more books by disabled creators (#OwnVoices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish more books by disabled creators so disabled perspectives are centered and harmful stereotypes are less likely to be perpetuated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues #OwnVoices creators are necessary to diversify publishing and that disabled creators are less likely to use harmful stereotypes. James Catchpole: 'we really need stories from the perspective of disabled children — stories that centre disabled characters.' Non-disabled writers can write well about disability, but industry should find and support disabled writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotyped 'disabled people are a burden' narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not portray disabled people as a burden to their families or rely on common harmful tropes that publishers expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jen Malia and interviewees note an industry expectation for stereotyped arcs; authors are sometimes pressured to insert such tropes and told editors 'can't connect to the story.' Authentic representation resists these stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'overcoming' or 'cure' narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid forcing stories where disabled characters must 'overcome' or be made better by losing/solving their disability; allow nuance and characters who embrace disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kati Gardner and others note publishers often prefer familiar tropes of overcoming adversity. The piece emphasizes that disability narratives are nuanced and should not be forced into narrow arc of overcoming or tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include disabled characters in stories that aren't 'about' disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish disabled characters incidentally in genres and plots (adventure, fantasy, friendship) where disability is not the central subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several publishers (Orca, Running Press, Candlewick) and authors encourage depiction of disabled characters even when the book isn’t specifically about disability. Tyler Feder: wants characters in stories about friendship or magic, not only explanatory books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent intersectional and multiple identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure disabled characters reflect intersecting identities of race, sexuality, class, gender, etc., rather than defaulting to white, straight, cis narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees note editorial boards are predominantly white (85%), producing mostly white disabled characters; recommend active seeking of disabled creators of color and stories centering multiple identities (example: Jessica Lewis/Jazz Taylor's Meow or Never).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire more disabled people across publishing (gatekeepers and staff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase hiring of disabled people as agents, editors, publicists, and leadership so decision-making reflects disabled perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple contributors state that decisions are made in a 'closed room' of non-disabled people; hiring disabled staff will let authentic stories be found and promoted. Remote work is cited as an important enabler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt individualized approaches to working with disabled people
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask creators what accommodations they need and be flexible—there is no one-size-fits-all checklist for disability accommodations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes: 'ask their authors what they need' and avoid treating disability as uniform. Examples include offering phone vs email, customizing processes, and respecting each person's needs throughout editorial and publicity processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make industry conferences and events accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure writing/publishing conferences include access (physical, remote, captioning, interpreters) so disabled writers can network and benefit from events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DVCon praised as accessible; authors report missed opportunities when conferences are inaccessible. Conference organizers should investigate and implement access measures to remove barriers to participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accessible ARCs, materials, and event access
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce accessible advanced review copies (ARCs), provide accessible online events and ensure promotional materials are available in accessible formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disabled creators often must request ARCs in accessible formats; publishers should proactively make ARCs and promotional assets accessible, and ensure accessibility when submitting work for awards and media promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design books with accessibility in mind (formats and design choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dyslexia-friendly fonts, cream-based paper to reduce contrast, accessible audiobooks with image descriptions, large print and braille/illustrated editions where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orca and Candlewick examples: dyslexia-friendly fonts, cream paper, audiobooks with image descriptions, licensing large print and braille illustrated editions. These features increase readership and inclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensitivity readers specialized in disability—but apply their feedback meaningfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Hire sensitivity/disability readers to check accuracy and harmful portrayals, but treat their work as substantive consultation rather than a checkbox exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quarto, Orca, Delacorte mentioned sensitivity readers; Tyler Feder's experience with Rabbi Ruti Regan shows concrete illustration adjustments. The author warns publishers sometimes do the minimum after receiving feedback; sensitivity readers should inform real changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage and coordinate with disability organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with national and international disability rights and advocacy organizations for training, outreach, and collaborative publishing initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sarah Allen suggests increased coordination for anti-ableist training, joint publishing, series selection, and broader outreach beyond the publishing 'bubble.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide staff training on ableism and disability awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Train editors, designers, and staff on ableism, representation, and practical accessibility (e.g., deaf awareness), integrated into editorial practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candlewick sent staff to a Highlights Foundation symposium and provided deaf awareness training in conjunction with a title release; such training can uncover colonial thinking and misrepresentation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include disabled characters in illustrations and group scenes intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Art direction should intentionally include characters with a range of mobility and visible diversity in group/scene illustrations so readers see themselves reflected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running Press example: creative direction ensures group scenes always include characters with a range of mobility enjoying themselves, playing, and engaging with the book's theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agents and editors should be willing to represent and work with disabled creators
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary agents and editors must not reject writers because they are disabled and should adapt processes to serve neurodiverse and disabled writers' needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author reports of agents declining after learning an author was disabled are cited as unacceptable. Jen Malia's agent accommodated autistic perspective in editing; Eric Smith's survey on serving neurodiverse writers recommended reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat disability as a specialist subject that requires research and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-disabled authors writing disabled characters should research and treat disability with the same seriousness as other specialist subjects, not as a literary device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James Catchpole: stop letting disability be used as crude metaphor or emotional manipulation; assume research is required (as with writing about other professions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tokenism and box-checking in inclusion efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not hire or consult disabled people merely to check a diversity box; integrate disabled voices into meaningful roles and decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cautions that sensitivity readers or one-off consultations should not substitute for hiring disabled staff or truly integrating disabled perspectives across processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure equitable promotion, publicity, and submission for awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide disabled creators with fair marketing budgets, ARC distribution, and submission to awards and media rather than relegating books to a perceived niche.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alaina Lavoie notes disabled creators may be denied promotional budgets, ARCs, or be labeled 'niche'; publishers should actively promote disabled voices and not assume limited marketability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create remote-friendly hiring and work policies to broaden access
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer remote or flexible roles and avoid requiring residency in specific cities (e.g., NYC) to remove employment barriers for disabled professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis of job listings at major houses showed very few remote-opportunities; remote work during the pandemic demonstrates feasibility and is a key inclusion measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track representation and industry data on disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor and report statistics on disabled characters in books and on disabled staff in publishing to identify gaps and measure progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to CCBC (3.4% disabled main characters in 2019) and Lee & Low workforce tracking demonstrate the need for ongoing measurement and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center agency and narrative centrality for disabled characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Make disabled children protagonists with real agency and plots, not sidelined examples or solely vehicles for moral messages like 'disabled kids are kids too.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James Catchpole criticizes stories that fail to center disabled characters or give them agency, leaving 'a slightly empty message' rather than a true plot; encourage full characterization and centrality.
